aquifer_vector.description:
Aquifer map for India generated with data from India Water Resources Information System (WRIS) ArcGIS portal. Ground water is the water present beneath the Earth’s surface in rock and soil pore spaces and in the fractures of rock formation. A unit of rock or an unconsolidated deposit is called an aquifer when it can yield a usable quantity of water. 

Based on the hydrogeological characteristics, the entire nation is divided into 14 principal aquifers: 
1. Alluvium
2. Laterite
3. Basalt
4. Sandstone
5. Shale
6. Limestone
7. Granite
8. Schist
9. Quartzite
10. Charnockite
11. Khondalite
12. Banded Gneissic Complex
13. Gneiss
14. Intrusive

Each major aquifer is uniquely identified by its region-specific aquifer properties such as aquifer thickness, specific yield, transmissivity and whether it is an unconfined and confined aquifer.

It is generated by aggregating the pixel-level tree canopy cover density (CCD) raster into area statistics, so each boundary contains the total area under low-density canopy, high-density canopy, and missing-data regions. change_detection_afforestation.description: This vector layer summarizes the area of tree cover gain within the selected MWS boundary over the analysis period. It is created by comparing the first and last three-year IndiaSAT land-use composites and aggregating the identified transitions to the MWS boundary. The output highlights conversions from built-up land, barren land, shrubland, and agricultural land into tree cover, indicating restoration, regeneration, and natural recovery within the planning unit.

area_in_ha.description: area in hectares identified as Tree Cover Gain

change_detection_cropintensity.description: This vector layer summarizes changes in agricultural land-use intensity within the selected MWS boundary over the analysis period. It is generated from IndiaSAT Land Use and Land Cover composites by comparing the first and last three-year composites and aggregating the crop-related class transitions to the MWS boundary. The output captures shifts among agricultural classes and helps quantify changes in cultivation intensity and land productivity within the study area.

area_in_ha.description: area in hectares identified for analysis

change_detection_deforestation.description: This vector layer summarizes the area of tree cover loss within the selected MWS boundary over the analysis period. It is derived from IndiaSAT Land Use and Land Cover composites by comparing the first three-year composite with the last three-year composite and aggregating the detected transitions to the MWS boundary. The output represents conversion from tree cover to built-up land, agricultural land, barren land, or shrubland, indicating deforestation within the planning unit.

area_in_ha.description: area in hectares identified as tree cover loss

change_detection_degradation.description: This vector layer summarizes the area affected by land degradation within the selected MWS boundary over the analysis period. It is generated from IndiaSAT Land Use and Land Cover composites by comparing the first and last three-year composites and aggregating the detected transitions to the MWS boundary. The output captures pixels where vegetated or productive land classes changed into built-up land, barren land, or scrub, indicating loss of ecological cover and declining land productivity.

change_detection_shrubchange.description: This vector layer summarizes changes in shrub and scrub-dominated areas within the selected MWS boundary over the analysis period. croppingDrought_kharif.description:
Drought frequency map for India. The Department of Agriculture, Cooperation & Farmers Welfare under the Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare, Government of India released the "Manual for Drought Management" in 2016 for the prevention, mitigation and management of droughts in India. The manual introduces scientific indices and parameters such as Vegetation Condition Index (VCI) for more accurate determination and assessment of drought. This map is an attempt to implement the methodology of the drought manual using various remote sensing products.

Following are the output classes in the model: 
1. Severe
2. Moderate
3. Mild

Input to the model is Rainfall data  (CHIRPS), Vegetation data (Landsat), Crop data (MODIS), Land use land cover (IndiaSAT). Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/tree/main/computing/drought).

drought_causality.description:
The Drought Causality layer is a yearly vector layer computed at the microwatershed scale. It is designed to identify the specific triggers and ecological/agricultural impacts of drought events, empowering rural communities to select targeted climate adaptation strategies. A year is declared a drought year for a microwatershed when it records more than 5 weeks of moderate or severe drought during the monsoon.

The layer combines meteorological triggers with impact indicators, all assessed week by week through the monsoon. The triggers are:

- Rainfall deviation from long-period averages,
- Dry spells (4 consecutive weeks, each with a rainfall deficit above 50%),
- The Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI).

The impact indicators are:

- The Vegetation Condition Index (VCI), from NDVI and NDWI,
- The Moisture Adequacy Index (MAI), the ratio of Actual Evapotranspiration (AET) to Potential Evapotranspiration (PET),
- The percentage of Kharif crop area sown.

Each moderate or severe drought week is mapped to its combination of trigger and impact. In declared drought years, these combinations are tallied to find the top three cause-and-impact pairs for each micro-watershed.

The results point to different responses:

- Rainfall-driven droughts suggest rainwater harvesting structures.
- Soil moisture decline suggests changing cropping patterns or adopting drought resistant crops.
- Crop health loss and reduced sown area signal severe agricultural impact, calling for longer-term strategies such as livelihood diversification.

hydrological_annual.description:
Annual water balance map for India. Data to compute the water balance for each microwatershed as rainfall - evapotranspiration - runoff, along with the specific yield obtained from aquifer data are used to estimate the change in depth to water. Note that this only takes the vertical flux into account and hence is likely to suffer from accuracy issues in the absence of accounting for lateral flow through the underlying aquifer. 

The vector data contains timeseries of annual mean precipitation (in mm), runoff (in mm), evapotranspiration (in mm), water balance (in mm), and cumulative water balance since 2017 as an indicator of cumulative surplus or deficit, for each microwatershed.

Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/blob/main/computing/mws/well_depth.py).

hydrological_seasonal.description:
Water balance with fortnightly temporal resolution for India. The vertical flux for a micro-watershed is computed as: Water Balance (ΔG) = Precipitation (P) - Runoff (Qout) - Evapotranspiration (ET). 

Precipitation data has been obtained from JAXA's Global Satellite Mapping of Precipitation (GSMaP), Evapotranspiration data from FLDAS Noah land Surface model by NASA and USGS, and runoff has been computed on a per-pixel using slope-adjusted CN numbers, the hydrological soil group, and LULC. Note that this only computes the vertical flux and does not account for sub-surface flows from adjacent micro-watersheds. 

The vector data contains timeseries of fortnightly mean precipitation (in mm), runoff (in mm), evapotranspiration (in mm), water balance (in mm), and cumulative water balance since 2017 as an indicator of cumulative surplus or deficit, for each microwatershed.

Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/tree/main/computing/mws).

livestock.description: Livestock are a central part of the rural economy -- a store of savings, insurance against crop failure, a daily income through milk, and a livelihood base for landless and marginal households. The Livestock Census, conducted periodically by the Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying together with the State Governments and Union Territories, is the principal source of livestock data in the country. This layer publishes village-level headcounts from the 20th Livestock Census (reference year 2019) for the five major species groups -- cattle, buffalo, sheep, goat, and pig. It complements the land, water, and facilities layers, since grazing pressure bears on commons and watershed health, livestock water demand matters for water budgeting, and dairy and meat production potential depends on the local livestock mix.

mws.description: Map of microwatershed connectivity for India. nrega_annual.description:
Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) assets categorization map for India. Permissible works under the scheme have been categorized from the natural resource management (NRM) lens through keyword matching, with the goal of helping in examining the current distribution of assets and facilitate the planning of new assets to ensure water security and sustainable livelihoods in rural India. 

The Pan India map is available from 2017 onwards. These are the classes in the current version of the map:
1. Soil and water conservation
2. Irrigation on farms
3. Other on-farm works
4. Plantations
5. Land restoration
6. Off-farm livelihood assets
7. Community assets

Input to the keyword matching algorithm is MGNREGS permissible work list and MGNREGA assets obtained from Bhuvan. Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/blob/main/computing/misc/nrega.py).

This layer contains one feature for each microwatershed. The clipped soil health rasters are used to calculate statistics for each microwatershed, summarising the spatial distribution of predicted soil nutrients and organic carbon within the selected microwatershed.

The vector layer includes the mean and percentile statistics for nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and organic carbon, along with the corresponding valid pixel counts. Where applicable, the OpenLandMap organic carbon baseline can also be included for comparison.

- N, P and K statistics: Reported in kg/ha.
- OC and OC_OLM statistics: Reported in percent (%).
- Mean: Average predicted soil property value across valid raster pixels within the microwatershed.
- Percentiles: 5th, 10th, 20th, 30th, 40th, 50th, 60th, 70th, 80th, 90th and 95th, where available in the output.
- Pixel count: Number of valid raster pixels used to calculate the statistics for each soil property.

soil_type.description:
The Soil Type / Soil Variables layer provides essential spatial datasets on the physical, chemical, and hydrological properties of soil across India. These datasets draw from the global dataset of the Harmonized World Soil Database (HWSD v1.2).

Key Components & Sub-Layers

- Soil Texture & Depth Profiles: Topsoil (0–30 cm) and subsoil (30–100 cm) texture classes based on sand, silt, and clay proportions using USDA classifications.
- Chemical & Physical Health: Measures topsoil and subsoil pH (acidity/alkalinity), Organic Carbon (OC), Bulk Density (compaction), and Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC) to determine nutrient storage and soil health.
- Hydrologic Soil Groups (HSGs): Categorizes soils into Groups A, B, C, and D based on infiltration rates and runoff potential.
- Drainage & Water Capacity: Details Soil Drainage Classes (ranging from excessively to very poorly drained) and Available Water Capacity (AWC) in mm/m for plant water uptake.

This data is also combined with waterbody census data (2023) to additionally get a capacity map for the waterbodies. terrain.description:
Terrain clusters map for India. Classes in the terrain raster map are grouped into five broad categories: plains, broad slopes, steep slopes, valleys and ridges. Percentage area under each category is computed for each microwatershed. Clustering process was applied to microwatersheds across diverse terrain blocks, including: Masalia, Angul, Mandalgarh, Pindwara, Mohanpur. The identified clusters are: 

1. Broad sloppy and hilly
2. Mostly plains
3. Mostly hills and valleys
4. Broad plains and slopes

Precomputed cluster centroids are used to assign terrain clusters to new microwatersheds. Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/tree/main/computing/terrain_descriptor).

tree_in_grassland.description:
Unlike dense forest systems, tree degradation in grasslands is more subtle and spatially fragmented, making it difficult to detect using conventional approaches.

To address this, we introduce a contextual and transition-based framework to monitor tree degradation within grassland ecosystems. By combining temporally smoothed Land Use Land Cover (LULC) data with neighbourhood-based classification, we identify trees within grassland contexts and track their transitions over time. This enables the detection of tree degradation such as conversion to barren land, cropland, or built-up areas.
